source.title: Variable-Width Transformers
source.authors: Zhaofeng Wu; Oliver Sieberling; Shawn Tan; Rameswar Panda; Yury Polyanskiy; Yoon Kim

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some extracted symbols and formulas are garbled, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares language-model loss across parameter-matched transformer width profiles, providing a conceptual test of whether architecture shape has little effect on loss. It does not reproduce the original scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The study also evaluates downstream benchmarks, but those comparisons do not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. The representation analyses in Sections 4.1–4.3 are not results on the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains parameter- and depth-matched transformers (200M–2B dense, 3B/1B MoE) with different layer-width profiles and reports loss. That bears on V4, whether architecture details at a fixed parameter count change loss only slightly. It also fits loss against pre-training FLOPs across four sizes, which bears on V1. The method is not the originals' own, so T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that parameter-matched ×-shaped variable-width transformers consistently get slightly lower loss than uniform-width baselines, with fewer FLOPs and a smaller KV cache. They present nonuniform width allocation as a promising, more resource-efficient way to scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares parameter-matched uniform and variable-width transformer architectures; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss varies with width profile and dimension-expansion method. The paper reports that no single bottleneck location/dimension ratio pair is consistently best, though ratio-based patterns are roughly similar across tested sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: The width profile shifts the fitted loss–compute exponent slightly: -0.0503 for ×-shaped versus -0.0498 for constant width. The authors suggest the gap may widen at scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural width allocation changes both the intercept and the exponent of compute scaling laws.

record.problems: The scaling fits cover only 200M–2B dense models, and model size, token count, and compute change together because training tokens are set to 50 times parameter count. The reported loss is training loss, treated by the authors as expected held-out loss because data are not repeated. No uncertainty is stated for the loss comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 5–9 and Sections 4.1–4.3 report representation and activation analyses rather than results on the claim versions. Table 3 reports downstream evaluations at selected model sizes, but does not test downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Parameters and tokens are never varied independently (tokens are fixed at 50× parameters). Compute covers only about two orders of magnitude, with four points per family.
No small-run fit is used to predict much larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
The global depth-to-width ratio and other architectural hyperparameters are not varied; depth is fixed per size.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
Downstream results are reported at two sizes only, not as a function of scale or loss.
No sensitivity of exponents to fitting or setup choices is tested, beyond a tiny exponent difference between architectures.

missing.what: Power-law fit of loss against average layer size: constant width 17×W^-0.246 (R² 0.999), ×-shaped 17×W^-0.252 (R² 1.000).
Loss-matched compute from the fitted curves: the ×-former reaches the 2B baseline loss (2.751) with 77.8% of the FLOPs and 85.1% of the average width.

record.verdict_notes: The reader marked the V4 rows 'partial' because the gains are modest. But V4 predicts that loss changes only slightly, and all differences are at most about 1.3%, so those rows are observed. The authors frame the paper as a challenge to uniform width rather than to Kaplan's shape claim, though they cite later work showing shape matters. Figure 3's numbers are in the extracted text, so R11–R13 are determinable.

versions.untested_parts: It fits loss against pre-training FLOPs, but does not independently vary parameters, tokens, and compute with the other quantities held non-bottlenecked.
No small-run fit is used to predict and then evaluate runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study does not find a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation across fixed compute budgets or measure how that allocation changes with compute.
The study compares selected width profiles and width-expansion methods; it does not broadly vary depth, width, and other architecture details.
No modalities beyond text or other training regimes such as repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer are tested.
Downstream tasks are evaluated for architecture comparisons, not for predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not systematically test sensitivity of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations to fitting choices, data, or training schedules.

tranche.reason: Parameter- and depth-matched width-profile comparisons test architecture sensitivity using a different experimental method; the study also fits loss against compute across four dense sizes.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. The extracted name '> <former' denotes the ×-shaped model; R7's Transformer baseline is the constant-width MoE. Fitted FLOP savings are not demonstrated wall-clock savings; Section 5 describes implementation overhead.

statements.correction: Small loss differences across parameter-matched dense and MoE models; V4 supports. Dense fitted curves: target loss 2.751; variable-width compute 77.8% of constant-width compute; approximately 22% saving.
statements.problem: The consistent gains and fitted compute saving are supported, but they do not establish a limits_scope verdict for V4's small-loss-change claim. The approximately 22% saving is fitted at the 2B dense baseline's loss, rather than established for every dense/MoE comparison.
